extracted.intended_audience: scientists and educated lay readers interested in solar physics and 19th-century physical theory
extracted.subtask_description: Presentation and defense of a physical theory of the Sun that proposes a cyclical dissociation–combustion mechanism for solar energy; the page sets out the necessary premises, supporting observations, experiments, and objections that a viable solar theory must meet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of interstellar gaseous and particulate matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Stellar space is supposed to be filled with highly rarefied gaseous bodies (hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon and their compounds) and solid materials in the form of dust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support cited includes meteorite analyses (occluded gases), spectrum analysis of cometary nuclei (Huggins et al.), and historical arguments (Grove, Humboldt, Zollner, Williams, Newton). The presence of such matter underpins the entire proposed mechanism and so is a fundamental requirement for the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical plausibility of a fan-like action due to solar rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Solar rotation within an unbounded medium produces a fan-like mechanical action drawing matter toward the poles and projecting it outward at the equator (equatorial outflow and polar inflow).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple mechanical argument (two equal gaseous masses at equal distances in equatorial vs polar positions) is provided to show that centrifugal forces break symmetry and produce a continuous current; this current's velocity depends on solar rotation rate. The fan action must be shown quantitatively to be compatible with observed dynamics (e.g., limited planetary retardation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capability of attenuated gaseous compounds to be dissociated by radiant solar energy
rubrics_metrics.description: Aqueous vapor and carbon compounds in extreme attenuation must be capable of being dissociated by solar radiation while in space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites laboratory experiments (vacuum tubes with platinum electrodes, solar exposure causing apparent hydrogen vacuum discharge), Tyndall's work on radiant heat, and the law of dissociation (Bunsen and Sainte-Claire Deville). This requirement calls for reproducible, quantitative laboratory demonstration that radiant energy dissociates such vapors under low pressure/density conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combustion/flare-up at the photosphere returning products of combustion to space
rubrics_metrics.description: Dissociated vapors drawn toward the Sun should be compressed and heated sufficiently at the photosphere to ignite, producing aqueous vapor and carbonic acid which are then driven toward the equator and projected into space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism details: inflowing hydrogen/hydrocarbons burn near photosphere; combustion products (denser gases) flow equatorially and are centrifugally projected outward. The theory must show this cycle is physically plausible and matches photospheric observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy-balance sufficiency (must supply solar radiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inflowing stream of dissociated vapors must be shown to provide sufficient heat when combusted to account for the known rate of solar radiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author provides a sample calculation assuming certain inflow densities and combustible fraction (1/20th), yielding heat-units per square foot comparable to Herschel/Pouillet measurements. A viable theory should include such quantitative estimates and address sensitivity to assumed parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with spectroscopic observations (hydrogen prevalence and absorption lines)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must account for the observed solar spectrum (prevalence of hydrogen lines and presence/absence of other substances' lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation offered: high solar temperatures dissociate heavier compounds (so they don't exist in photosphere), while dissociation in space and neutral atmospheres can neutralize or hide spectral lines. The theory should reconcile where metallic vapors are observed and how lines may be neutralized by intervening gases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of metallic vapors and multi-layer solar atmospheres
rubrics_metrics.description: Metallic vapors observed by spectroscope are attributed to a lower, denser solar atmosphere separate from the lighter photosphere; these layers must be dynamically and chemically consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author proposes a dense metallic atmosphere that does not participate in fan action, with an intermediate neutral 'penumbra' preventing excessive intermixture. Vortices and explosive effects at interfaces should explain observed 'stormy regions' (sunspot zones). Theory must account for how metallic vapors persist and how interlayer friction behaves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of zodiacal light and particle luminosity
rubrics_metrics.description: A viable theory should furnish a consistent explanation of the zodiacal light, attributing its source to solar-outflow particles (dust) that are luminous either by reflected sunlight, phosphorescence, or slow electric discharge from electrified dust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author revives Mairan's view modified by continuous equatorial outflow to meet Laplace's objection. Guidance includes dust electrification examples (Siemens) and potential electric discharge mechanisms. The theory should match extent and luminosity characteristics of zodiacal light.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of cometary phenomena (nucleus, coma, tail)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must harmonize cometary observations: nuclei as aggregates absorbing gases, ignition/combustion near perihelion, luminous coma on forward side, and luminous tail composed of stellar dust radiating/reflexing combined sun+comet light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author models cometary behavior via occluded gases in stones, frictional heating leading to gas expulsion and zones of intense combustion (Huggins' observations). The tail formation is explained by luminous dust; a valid theory should predict these observable comet features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with geological carbonic-acid/CO2 requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should account for Earth's geological carbonic acid (CO2) budget—how enormous carbonate deposits and coal beds could be explained by an external supply rather than purely terrestrial sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author suggests Earth sits in the outflowing solar current and receives a steady influx of carbonic acid (citing Reiset/Dumas). A successful theory should quantify fluxes and show plausibility relative to geological estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical support from meteorite and vacuum-tube gas analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evidence such as occluded gases in meteorites (hydrogen-rich analyses) and behavior of vacuum-tubes (attenuated vapors turning into hydrogen-tubes) is required to support the premise that interplanetary matter contains dissociable gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites Dr. Flight's meteorite gas composition and Piazzi Smyth's vacuum-tube/spectral memoirs; a defensible theory should collect and interpret such chemical/spectroscopic data and address alternative explanations (e.g., contamination during atmospheric entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory reproducibility and quantitative demonstration of dissociation
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative experiments must be developed into quantitative, reproducible laboratory demonstrations showing dissociation of aqueous vapor and carbonic acid by radiation under low pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author describes glass-tube experiments with platinum electrodes, refrigeration of one end, solar exposure, and inferred hydrogen discharge; notes limitations (glass absorbs UV) and plans for Sprengel-pump gas collection. The criterion calls for rigorous experimental design, measurement of produced gas quantities, and controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of perpetual-motion-like conclusions; account for irrecoverable losses
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must not amount to perpetual motion; it must acknowledge irrecoverable losses (e.g., solar energy used on Earth via vegetation) and energy costs of sustaining circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author explicitly guards against critics' perpetual-motion charge, noting absolute loss of energy expended on Earth and tidal dissipation; any proposed recycling mechanism must quantify net gains versus inevitable losses and show realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction and correspondence with observed solar structural features (corona, stormy regions, streams)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should predict solar structural features (an ideal corona with accumulation of igneous matter, vortices, outbursts of metallic vapors, equatorial streams) and these predictions should correspond to observational reports (e.g., Proctor, eyewitness accounts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author presented a diagram of such an ideal corona to the Royal Society and seeks corroboration from solar observers. A viable theory must connect its schematic structures to telescopic and spectroscopic observations of the corona and active regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical and thermo-physical plausibility using dissociation laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory's chemical steps must follow known dissociation laws: the point of decomposition of compounds depends on temperature and pressure (Bunsen, Sainte-Claire Deville), and radiant heat can have dissociating power beyond measurable thermometer temperatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author invokes Sainte-Claire Deville's dissociation tensions (e.g., aqueous vapor at 2800°C at atm. pressure) and Tyndall's findings on radiant heat absorption; the theory must correctly apply these laws to solar/photospheric/space conditions and justify where dissociation occurs (in space vs photosphere) given pressure–temperature relationships.
